separation-lab.title: Choose a separation route
separation-lab.intro: Choose a method from the physical properties of the components. Each scenario has a different substance to recover.

questions.name: Sand and salt
questions.prompt: Sand and salt are mixed. Water dissolves the salt but not the sand. After adding water and stirring, how should you collect the sand?
questions.explanation: Sand remains as the residue. Dissolved salt passes through the filter with the water.

questions.name: Recover salt
questions.prompt: After filtering off sand, how can you recover solid salt from the filtrate if collecting the water is unnecessary?
options: Evaporate water and crystallize the salt
questions.answer: Evaporate water and crystallize the salt
questions.explanation: Removing solvent allows the dissolved salt to crystallize. Dissolved ions pass through an ordinary filter.

questions.name: Two miscible liquids
questions.prompt: Two miscible liquids have different but relatively close boiling points. Which method is best suited to separating them?
questions.explanation: Repeated vaporization and condensation in a fractionating column improves separation. A separating funnel is used for immiscible liquid layers.

isotope-mixtures.title: Work backwards from an isotope average
isotope-mixtures.intro: Use a fictional element X with only two isotopes, of relative isotopic masses 20.0 and 22.0. Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean, not a mass number.

questions.name: Weighted mean
questions.prompt: X-20 has abundance 75.0% and X-22 has abundance 25.0%. Find the relative atomic mass.
questions.explanation: 20.0 × 0.750 + 22.0 × 0.250 = 20.5. The more abundant isotope contributes more to the average.

questions.name: Find an abundance
questions.prompt: Another sample has relative atomic mass 21.2. What percentage of its atoms are X-22?
questions.explanation: Let f be the fraction of X-22. 20(1 − f) + 22f = 21.2, giving f = 0.600, or 60.0%.

questions.name: Check a claim
questions.prompt: A sample containing only these two isotopes is reported to have relative atomic mass 23.0. Is this possible?
options: No, the mean must lie between 20.0 and 22.0
Yes, if X-22 is very abundant
Yes, because the isotope masses are added
questions.answer: No, the mean must lie between 20.0 and 22.0
questions.explanation: A weighted mean with non-negative abundances cannot lie outside the range of its constituent values.

emission-spectra.title: Read an electron transition
emission-spectra.intro: Connect discrete energy levels with line emission spectra. These questions concern photons and transitions rather than filling orbitals.

questions.name: Emit or absorb?
questions.prompt: An electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level. What happens?
questions.explanation: The atom emits a photon with energy equal to the difference between the two levels.

questions.name: Compare photons
questions.prompt: Transition A has a larger energy gap than transition B. How does the emitted photon from A compare?
options: Same frequency but greater speed in vacuum
questions.explanation: E = hf and c = fλ. Greater photon energy means greater frequency and shorter wavelength; the speed in vacuum is unchanged.

questions.name: Why lines?
questions.prompt: Why does an isolated atomic gas produce discrete spectral lines rather than every possible wavelength?
options: Only specific electron energy differences are allowed
Every atom emits only one photon colour
questions.answer: Only specific electron energy differences are allowed
questions.explanation: Quantized energy levels allow only particular transition energies, producing characteristic wavelengths.

ionic-formulas.title: Build a neutral ionic formula
ionic-formulas.intro: Balance total positive and negative charge using the simplest whole-number ratio. Keep polyatomic ions together.

questions.name: Magnesium chloride
questions.prompt: Which formula combines Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ in a neutral compound?
questions.explanation: One Mg²⁺ requires two Cl⁻ ions: +2 + 2(−1) = 0.

questions.name: Aluminium oxide
questions.prompt: Which formula combines Al³⁺ and O²⁻ in the simplest neutral ratio?
questions.explanation: Two aluminium ions give +6 and three oxide ions give −6. The simplest ratio is 2:3.

questions.name: Calcium nitrate
questions.prompt: Which formula combines Ca²⁺ with nitrate, NO₃⁻?
questions.explanation: Two nitrate ions balance one calcium ion. Parentheses show that the entire NO₃ group occurs twice.

shape-polarity.title: Separate bond polarity from molecular polarity
shape-polarity.intro: Use electron domains and symmetry to predict molecular shape and whether bond dipoles cancel. Multiple bonds count as one electron domain in VSEPR.

questions.name: Carbon dioxide
questions.prompt: CO₂ has two bonding domains and no lone pairs on its central carbon. Which description is correct?
questions.explanation: The two polar C=O bonds point in opposite directions in a linear molecule, so their equal dipoles cancel.

questions.name: Water
questions.prompt: H₂O has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs around oxygen. What is its molecular shape and polarity?
questions.explanation: Four electron domains have a tetrahedral arrangement, but the molecular shape describes atom positions: bent. The O–H dipoles do not cancel.

questions.name: Ammonia
questions.prompt: NH₃ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around nitrogen. What is its molecular shape?
questions.explanation: Four electron domains surround nitrogen. One is a lone pair, leaving three bonds arranged in a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.

metallic-properties.title: Explain a metal's properties
metallic-properties.intro: Use the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons to explain behaviour beyond electrical conduction.

questions.name: Malleability
questions.prompt: Why can a pure metal often be hammered into a sheet without immediately shattering?
options: Attraction to delocalized electrons persists as ion layers move
Its atoms turn into neutral gas molecules
questions.answer: Attraction to delocalized electrons persists as ion layers move
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is not restricted to fixed pairs of atoms. The structure can deform while attractive interactions remain.

questions.name: Charge
questions.prompt: In the simple metallic bonding model, is a bulk sample of metal electrically charged?
options: No, the positive ions and delocalized electrons balance
questions.answer: No, the positive ions and delocalized electrons balance
questions.explanation: The model separates positive ionic cores and mobile electrons, but their total charges cancel in a neutral metal sample.

questions.name: Bond strength
questions.prompt: In a simplified comparison with similar ion sizes, which change tends to strengthen metallic bonding?
options: More delocalized electrons per atom and higher positive ion charge
Increasing ion separation while holding charge fixed
questions.answer: More delocalized electrons per atom and higher positive ion charge
questions.explanation: Stronger electrostatic attraction can result from increased positive charge and electron density. Real melting points also depend on structure; this is a model trend.

periodic-oxides.title: Predict oxide behaviour
periodic-oxides.intro: Connect metallic and non-metallic character to acid–base behaviour of period 3 oxides. Aluminium oxide provides an important exception to a simple two-way classification.

questions.name: Sodium oxide
questions.prompt: Na₂O reacts with water to form NaOH. How is this oxide classified?
questions.explanation: Sodium oxide is a basic oxide. Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH gives an alkaline solution.

questions.name: Sulfur trioxide
questions.prompt: SO₃ reacts with water to form sulfuric acid. How is this oxide classified?
questions.explanation: Sulfur trioxide is an acidic non-metal oxide. SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

questions.name: Aluminium oxide
questions.prompt: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases. Which term describes this behaviour?
questions.explanation: An amphoteric oxide can react with either acids or bases. This does not mean that it dissolves readily in water.

organic-isomers.title: Distinguish formulas and isomers
organic-isomers.intro: Compare molecular formulas with atom connectivity. A different way of writing the same connectivity is not a new structural isomer.

questions.name: Same formula, different group
questions.prompt: CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃OCH₃ both have molecular formula C₂H₆O. What is their relationship?
questions.explanation: They have the same molecular formula but different connectivity: one is an alcohol, the other an ether.

questions.name: Branching
questions.prompt: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and (CH₃)₃CH are examples of which relationship?
questions.explanation: Both have formula C₄H₁₀. One has an unbranched chain and the other a branched carbon skeleton.

questions.name: Count carbon atoms
questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
questions.explanation: Count the first CH₃, the CH₂, the carbonyl carbon in COO, and the final CH₃: four carbons in total.

calorimetry-errors.title: Diagnose a calorimetry result
calorimetry-errors.intro: Distinguish heat transfer, molar enthalpy and systematic heat loss using fictional calorimeter measurements.

questions.name: Heat loss
questions.prompt: An exothermic reaction loses heat to the room, but the calculation uses only the solution's temperature rise. How does the calculated ΔH compare with the true value?
questions.explanation: The measured temperature rise is too small, so the calculated heat released is too small in magnitude. The result is closer to zero.

questions.name: Include the container
questions.prompt: The solution absorbs 2.00 kJ and the calorimeter absorbs 0.30 kJ. Assume no other heat transfer. Find q for the reaction.
questions.explanation: q(reaction) = −[q(solution) + q(calorimeter)] = −(2.00 + 0.30) = −2.30 kJ.

questions.name: Scale the reaction
questions.prompt: Twice as much reactant undergoes the same reaction under the same conditions. What happens to the molar enthalpy change?
questions.explanation: Total heat doubles, but dividing by twice the reacted amount gives the same enthalpy change per mole.

formation-enthalpy.title: Calculate from formation enthalpies
formation-enthalpy.intro: Use ΔH°reaction = ΣνΔH°f(products) − ΣνΔH°f(reactants). All supplied values for the fictional substances are in kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.name: One-to-one reaction
questions.prompt: For A → B, ΔH°f(A) = −80 and ΔH°f(B) = −140. Calculate ΔH°reaction.
questions.explanation: Products minus reactants: −140 − (−80) = −60 kJ mol⁻¹ for the reaction as written.

questions.name: Use the coefficients
questions.prompt: For 2A → B, ΔH°f(A) = −80 and ΔH°f(B) = −140. Calculate ΔH°reaction for the equation as written.
questions.explanation: −140 − 2(−80) = +20 kJ mol⁻¹. Multiply each formation enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient.

questions.name: Reference state
questions.prompt: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state?
questions.explanation: It is zero by convention. This does not mean every compound has zero formation enthalpy, or that all physical forms of an element have zero values.

fuel-cells.title: Compare a fuel cell with combustion
fuel-cells.intro: Consider hydrogen as an energy carrier and distinguish what happens inside a device from the environmental effects of producing its fuel.

questions.name: Energy conversion
questions.prompt: What is the main useful energy conversion in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
options: Electrical energy to stored hydrogen only
Chemical energy directly to electrical energy
questions.answer: Chemical energy directly to electrical energy
questions.explanation: Separated electrode reactions transfer electrons through an external circuit. Heat is also produced; the cell is not perfectly efficient.

questions.name: Overall product
questions.prompt: In the ideal overall reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of water form from 0.60 mol H₂ with excess O₂?
questions.explanation: The H₂:H₂O ratio is 1:1, so 0.60 mol hydrogen forms 0.60 mol water.

questions.name: Production matters
questions.prompt: A fuel cell produces water during use. Does that alone establish that its hydrogen has zero associated carbon emissions?
options: No, the hydrogen production and energy sources also matter
Yes, all hydrogen production is emission-free
Yes, the device destroys all carbon dioxide
questions.answer: No, the hydrogen production and energy sources also matter
questions.explanation: Hydrogen can be produced through different processes. Assessing environmental impact requires considering production and energy supply as well as use.

entropy-changes.title: Account for entropy changes (AHL)
entropy-changes.intro: Predict changes in energy and matter dispersal, then use supplied fictional standard molar entropies. Keep entropy units separate from enthalpy units.

questions.name: Vaporization
questions.prompt: What is the usual sign of the system's entropy change when a liquid vaporizes at its boiling point?
questions.explanation: The gas has many more accessible arrangements than the liquid. The system's entropy increases even though liquid and gas can coexist at equilibrium.

questions.name: Calculate ΔS°
questions.prompt: For A → 2B, S°(A) = 120 and S°(B) = 90 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔS° for the reaction as written.
questions.explanation: ΔS° = 2(90) − 120 = +60 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Entropy changes include the stoichiometric coefficients.

questions.name: Temperature dependence
questions.prompt: A reaction has ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0. Assuming these signs remain unchanged, when is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS negative?
questions.explanation: The enthalpy term is negative and subtracting positive TΔS makes ΔG still more negative. This predicts thermodynamic favourability, not reaction speed.

yield-economy.title: Separate yield from atom economy
yield-economy.intro: Use fictional reaction data to distinguish recovered product from how efficiently a balanced reaction directs reactant mass into the desired product.

questions.name: Percentage yield
questions.prompt: The theoretical product mass is 8.00 g and the isolated product mass is 6.00 g. Find the percentage yield.
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = actual / theoretical × 100 = 6.00 / 8.00 × 100 = 75.0%.

questions.name: Atom economy
questions.prompt: In A + B → P + Q, P is the desired product. For the stoichiometric quantities shown, the total reactant mass is 100 g and the theoretical mass of P is 70 g. Find the atom economy.
questions.explanation: Atom economy = theoretical mass of desired product / total stoichiometric reactant mass × 100 = 70%. It is determined by the reaction, not by product recovery.

questions.name: Interpret both metrics
questions.prompt: A reaction has 100% yield but 50% atom economy. What does this mean?
options: All theoretical desired product was recovered, but half the stoichiometric reactant mass forms other products
Half the desired product was lost
questions.answer: All theoretical desired product was recovered, but half the stoichiometric reactant mass forms other products
questions.explanation: Yield measures recovery relative to a theoretical amount. Atom economy measures how reactant mass is distributed among products.

rate-orders.title: Infer a rate equation (AHL)
rate-orders.intro: Use invented initial-rate comparisons at constant temperature. Change only one reactant concentration at a time; do not infer reaction orders from overall equation coefficients.

questions.name: Order in A
questions.prompt: Doubling [A] while holding all other reactant concentrations fixed makes the initial rate four times larger. Find the order with respect to A.
questions.explanation: 2 to the power m equals 4, so m = 2. The reaction is second order with respect to A.

questions.name: Order in B
questions.prompt: Tripling [B] with all other reactant concentrations fixed leaves the initial rate unchanged. Find the order with respect to B.
questions.explanation: 3 to the power zero equals 1. The measured rate is zero order with respect to B over these conditions.

questions.name: Rate constant
questions.prompt: The measured rate law is rate = k[A]². At [A] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.012 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Calculate k.
questions.explanation: k = 0.012 / (0.20)² = 0.300 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. The rate-constant units depend on the overall order.

equilibrium-shifts.title: Distinguish a shift from a change in K
equilibrium-shifts.intro: Consider N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), with an exothermic forward reaction. Predict the response to one changed condition at a time.

questions.name: Compress the mixture
questions.prompt: The equilibrium mixture is compressed at constant temperature. Which net change restores equilibrium?
options: Formation of more N₂ and H₂
No response because pressure never matters
questions.explanation: The forward direction reduces gas amount from four stoichiometric moles to two. K remains unchanged at fixed temperature.

questions.name: Raise temperature
questions.prompt: For this exothermic forward reaction, what happens when temperature increases?
options: Equilibrium shifts right and K increases
Equilibrium shifts left and K decreases
questions.answer: Equilibrium shifts left and K decreases
questions.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic reverse direction. Temperature changes the equilibrium constant, unlike a concentration or pressure change at fixed temperature.

questions.name: Add a catalyst
questions.prompt: A catalyst is added to a mixture already at equilibrium at fixed temperature. What changes?
options: Both forward and reverse rates increase, but equilibrium composition is unchanged
questions.answer: Both forward and reverse rates increase, but equilibrium composition is unchanged
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a faster pathway in both directions. It does not change the equilibrium constant or favour one equilibrium composition.

titration-stoichiometry.title: Use a titration endpoint
titration-stoichiometry.intro: Use fictional acid–base measurements. Assume the measured endpoint closely matches equivalence and the stated neutralization is complete.

questions.name: Convert volume
questions.prompt: A titre is 25.0 cm³. Express it in dm³ before using n = cV.

questions.name: Find concentration
questions.prompt: 20.0 cm³ of HCl is neutralized by 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Using HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, find the HCl concentration.

questions.name: Two protons
questions.prompt: For complete neutralization, H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. How many moles of NaOH are required for 0.0030 mol H₂SO₄?
questions.explanation: The mole ratio H₂SO₄:NaOH is 1:2, so 2 × 0.0030 = 0.0060 mol NaOH is required.

voltaic-cells.title: Trace charge through a voltaic cell
voltaic-cells.intro: Use a zinc–copper cell operating spontaneously: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Distinguish electrons in the wire from ions in solution.

questions.name: Anode reaction
questions.prompt: Which half-equation occurs at the anode?
questions.explanation: Oxidation occurs at the anode. Zinc atoms release electrons and enter solution as Zn²⁺.

questions.name: External circuit
questions.prompt: In which direction do electrons flow through the external wire?
options: Through the salt bridge from copper to zinc
From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
questions.answer: From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
questions.explanation: Electrons released by zinc oxidation travel through the wire to the copper electrode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced.

questions.name: Salt bridge
questions.prompt: What is the main role of the salt bridge?
options: Allow ion migration to maintain charge balance
questions.answer: Allow ion migration to maintain charge balance
questions.explanation: Ions migrate to prevent charge build-up in each half-cell. Electron transfer between electrodes occurs in the external circuit.

radical-products.title: Predict radical products and limitations
radical-products.intro: Apply radical chain ideas to methane chlorination under UV light. Think about atom conservation, side products and why a single pure product is difficult to obtain.

questions.name: Regenerate the carrier
questions.prompt: Complete CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + ?
questions.explanation: A chlorine radical is regenerated, allowing another propagation step. Both chlorine atoms are accounted for.

questions.name: Combine methyl radicals
questions.prompt: Which product forms when two CH₃• radicals combine in a termination step?
questions.explanation: The two carbon-centred radicals form a C–C bond: CH₃• + •CH₃ → CH₃CH₃. No radical remains.

questions.name: Further substitution
questions.prompt: Why can methane chlorination produce CH₂Cl₂ as well as CH₃Cl?
options: The first substitution product can undergo further substitution
Chlorine atoms turn into carbon atoms
Every initiation step makes CH₂Cl₂ directly
questions.answer: The first substitution product can undergo further substitution
questions.explanation: CH₃Cl still contains C–H bonds. Further radical substitution can replace additional hydrogen atoms, giving a mixture of products.

substitution-mechanisms.title: Compare substitution mechanisms (AHL)
substitution-mechanisms.intro: Compare idealized SN1 and SN2 mechanisms in suitable conditions. The labels describe the molecularity of the rate-determining step, not the number of products.

questions.name: SN2 concentration change
questions.prompt: An SN2 reaction follows rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]. Both concentrations are doubled at fixed temperature. By what factor does the rate change?
questions.explanation: Doubling each of the two first-order concentration terms multiplies the rate by 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.name: SN1 intermediate
questions.prompt: Which species is the characteristic intermediate in the idealized SN1 substitution of a tertiary halogenoalkane?
questions.explanation: The leaving group departs in the slow first step, forming a carbocation. The nucleophile then attacks the electron-deficient carbon.

questions.name: SN2 stereochemistry
questions.prompt: An SN2 reaction occurs at a chiral carbon. What is the characteristic stereochemical outcome at that centre?
options: A planar carbocation must form first
No change in the arrangement of bonds
questions.explanation: Backside nucleophilic attack and simultaneous leaving-group departure invert the spatial arrangement at the reacting carbon.
